title: Rainy day restaurant phone orders: how to handle the spike

description: Rainy day restaurant phone orders rise when guests stay home. Use call forwarding, better scripts, and faster order flow to keep sales up.
question: How should I handle rainy day restaurant phone orders when the phone starts ringing nonstop?
answer: Rainy nights usually bring more pickup and delivery calls, so the main job is to answer fast, quote ready times clearly, and keep the line moving. Set up call forwarding for busy or unanswered calls, use a simple order script, and make sure a phone host can take the basic details from your live menu while staff handle tricky calls.

intro:
Rainy day restaurant phone orders usually go up because more guests stay home and call for pickup or delivery. The fix is simple: make sure someone answers, the order process is short, and your ready times stay realistic.

For many independent spots, that means forwarding the phone when the line is busy, using a clear script, and having a backup for overflow. ROAL can help here because it answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: Why do rainy nights bring more phone orders?
sections.body:
Bad weather changes how people eat. Some guests do not want to drive. Some do not want to wait in a lobby. Others decide at the last minute that they want pizza, wings, sandwiches, or family takeout.

That means the phone can jump fast on a rainy evening, especially around dinner. A good plan is to treat weather like a mini rush, the same way you treat Friday night or game day.

Use this simple prep list before the storm hits:
- Check that hours, address, parking notes, and menu items are current.
- Decide who answers the phone first.
- Decide when calls should forward if the line is busy.
- Set a realistic ready-time range for pickup and delivery.
- Make sure sold-out items are marked sold out.

A useful phone line is: "Thanks for calling. We’re busy tonight, but I can take your order right now." That one sentence reassures the caller and moves the call forward.

sections.h2: What should my team say on a rainy-night call?
sections.body:
Rainy calls work best when the script is short. The goal is to get the order, give a ready time, and confirm the details without a lot of back-and-forth.

A strong script for a busy night looks like this:
1. Greet the caller.
2. Ask whether it is pickup or delivery.
3. Take the items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
4. Collect the name and phone number.
5. Give the ready time.
6. Repeat the full order back.

Example line: "I have one large pepperoni, one chicken parm sub, extra crispy fries, and a two-topping salad. Your name and phone number, please."

If you use ROAL, it can take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the restaurant’s live menu, then confirm the order back before sending a ticket to the kitchen screen. It also speaks the caller’s language and can take reservation requests. That helps on rainy nights when the line is busy and the front counter is already full.

Keep one rule in mind: tricky calls still go to staff. Allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests should be handed off with a clear summary.

sections.h2: How do I set up call forwarding for stormy nights?
sections.body:
Call forwarding is one of the easiest ways to protect rainy-night sales. You can forward all calls, or just the ones that are unanswered or busy.

The exact code depends on the carrier or phone system, so always confirm with your provider and test with a real call. Common examples in the US include:

| Situation | Common code examples |
|---|---|
| Forward all calls on some landlines | *72, then the forwarding number; *73 to turn it off |
| AT&T / T-Mobile GSM | **21*number# to forward all calls; ##21# to turn it off |
| Unanswered calls | **61*number# |
| Busy calls | **67*number# |
| Verizon Wireless | *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding |
| Business VoIP systems | Usually set in the web portal |

A practical setup is to forward busy calls during the dinner rush and turn it off when the weather clears. If you want a carrier-by-carrier cheat sheet, ROAL has [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

Example: if your line gets 12 calls in an hour and you can only answer 7, forwarding the overflow can save the 5 calls that would otherwise hit voicemail.

sections.h2: What menu and staff prep should happen before the rain starts?
sections.body:
A rainy shift gets easier when the menu is ready for fast ordering. People ordering from home often want comfort food, repeats, and simple add-ons. That means you should review sold-out items, popular modifiers, and any late-night limits before the rush.

Use this short prep checklist:
- Make sure the live menu matches what you can actually cook tonight.
- Update hours if you are closing early.
- Confirm which sides, sizes, and add-ons are available.
- Decide who handles manager calls and allergy-sensitive questions.
- Put the kitchen screen where staff can see live tickets quickly.

If you use ROAL, the owner can paste the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or "Name, City" at /try. ROAL reads public menu pages, menu PDFs, menu photos, hours, and address, then builds a phone host in about a minute. The owner can test-call it in the browser with no sign-up needed.

A useful staff line is: "We’re adjusting for the weather tonight, so I’m checking the current ready time now." That buys a few seconds and keeps expectations realistic.

sections.h2: How can I keep rainy calls from turning into missed revenue?
sections.body:
The biggest risk on a rainy night is not that the phone rings. It is that a caller gives up after no answer, a long hold, or a confusing menu. A simple backup plan keeps the order moving even when the front counter is slammed.

Here’s a practical rainy-night workflow:
1. Answer the first ring if you can.
2. Forward busy or unanswered calls to a backup line when needed.
3. Keep the menu tight and current.
4. Confirm the caller’s name, number, and ready time.
5. Send the kitchen a clean ticket.
6. Save questions you could not answer in an inbox so the host learns them later.

sections.h2: What should I check after the rush ends?
sections.body:
After the rain stops, look at the calls while the night is still fresh. You do not need a long report. You just need to see where calls slowed down, where staff got stuck, and which questions came up again and again.

Review these items:
- Which calls were answered and which were missed.
- Whether the quoted ready times were realistic.
- Which items were requested most often.
- Whether allergy or manager calls reached the right person.
- Whether the kitchen tickets were clean and readable.

A simple review question is: "Did we make it easy for a caller to place the order in under a minute?" If the answer is no, shorten the greeting, remove outdated menu items, and tighten the call handoff.

For owners who want a broader view of weather and holidays, ROAL also has related posts on [holiday phone orders without the chaos](/blog/holiday-phone-orders-restaurant) and [after-hours calls](/use-cases/after-hours). Those situations often create the same problem: more calls than your counter can comfortably handle.

takeaways: Rainy nights usually bring more pickup and delivery calls, so plan for a mini rush.
Use a short script, clear ready times, and current menu info to keep calls moving.
Call forwarding can catch overflow when your line gets busy or unanswered.
ROAL can answer routine orders, while tricky calls still go to staff.

faq.q: Why do rainy day restaurant phone orders increase?
faq.a: Rain usually keeps more guests at home, so they call for pickup or delivery instead of coming in. It can also push orders later into the evening as people decide not to drive. That is why rainy nights often behave like a rush period.

faq.q: Should I forward my restaurant phone on rainy nights?
faq.a: Yes, if you expect the line to get busy or you do not have enough staff to answer quickly. You can forward all calls or only unanswered and busy calls, depending on your carrier or phone system. Always test it with a real call before a storm hits.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take orders from my real menu?
faq.a: ROAL can read your live menu and take pickup and delivery orders from it. It handles items, sizes, modifiers, notes, caller name, phone number, and ready time, then sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It does not take card numbers over the phone.

faq.q: What calls should still go to staff on a rainy night?
faq.a: Allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests should go to staff. The phone host can pass along a summary so your team gets context fast. That keeps the front counter from getting stuck on calls that need a human decision.
